draft.briefing: Hey, you're at Ajanta Caves! These are 30 rock-cut Buddhist caves carved into a 75 m wall of rock, some dating back to the second century BCE. The paintings inside are counted among the finest surviving examples of ancient Indian art.
draft.hungryLine: There are no named eateries in my notes for the caves, so go for Maharashtrian classics like vada pav, kanda pohe or a spicy misal pav.

moodReplies.show-me-around: The caves are a 2 min walk from here. Look for the paintings of the Buddha's past lives and the tales from Aryasura's Jatakamala.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Find a quiet spot in one of the old viharas, the monasteries where monks once sat out the monsoon.
moodReplies.surprise-me: These caves weren't just for monks. Old records say merchants and pilgrims also rested here on their travels.

tips.title: Read the gestures.
tips.body: The paintings tell their stories through gesture, pose and form, so take your time on the faces and hands.

tips.title: Plan around February.
tips.body: The Ellora Ajanta Festival of classical dance and music usually happens in February, with dates that vary by year.

story.title: The first caves
story.body: The first phase of carving started around the second century BCE. Monks cut monasteries and worship halls into a 75 m wall of rock.

story.title: A second burst
story.body: Older accounts put the second phase between 400 and 650 CE. Later scholarship says it happened in a short window, around 460 to 480 CE.

story.title: A rainy-season retreat
story.body: Texts suggest monks stayed here through the monsoon. Merchants and pilgrims also stopped to rest along the way.

story.title: Soegaon gets its taluka
story.body: Soegaon, the town at the base of the Ajanta hills, became the headquarters of a new tahsil in 1953. Villages from Sillod and Kannad talukas were moved into it.

story.title: World Heritage
story.body: Ajanta is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its paintings and sculptures are seen as masterpieces of Buddhist religious art.
